title: Is the Heart Taken Captive?
intro: Husam al-Dosari opens with a lover whose heart is pulled between a smile and a rebuff. Soon the heart, reason and grey hair are each speaking, and the lover tells the very voice that could wake him up to go back to sleep. The poem widens from the promises a lover hears to the promises that time seems to make. Its last king needs no riches, only the contentment to enjoy his share and the freedom to give from it.

translation: Is the heart taken captive, or does it die of sickness,
when graceful women enter it and deem my blood theirs to shed?
1.sharh: Captivity and bloodshed belong to the language of power, sickness to that of the body. The lover tries both languages to describe how completely beauty has taken possession of him.

translation: They drew it from the covering that kept it cool
and wrapped it in a sash woven from embers.
2.sharh: The women replace the heart’s natural wrapping with an article of dress. It still looks protected, while every thread of its new sash burns.

translation: My heart spends the night tormented by contradiction,
closeness then estrangement, opposites that bend my resolve.
3.sharh: It takes only the small word “then” to undo the closeness he thought he had won. This repeated reversal wears down his capacity to make up his mind.

translation: They brought it fragrance at dawn and hurt at dusk.
It spends its evenings and mornings between scent and pain.
4.sharh: Morning and evening trade positions when the line turns. The ear comes back to where it started, like the heart that has to live this day over again.

translation: Their coldness gnawed at my very liver and left them unmoved.
When they smiled, light struck us from every side.
5.sharh: In Arabic poetry the liver can be the seat of deep feeling. Their refusal wounds him there, but even their favour strikes him like a burst of overwhelming light.

translation: With difficulty I shielded my eyes from her dark lips’ radiance.
I guard the ties of my resolve more than my eyes.
6.sharh: The woman is named by the admired dark tint of her lips. Looking away costs effort because it is the bonds holding his own will together that he is trying to protect.

translation: Union never kept me company by night to share a cup,
and when they turn away my words desert my mouth.
7.sharh: Union is an absent drinking companion, someone with whom he would have liked to talk late into the night. Rejection estranges him even from his own speech.

translation: And will the heart turn away if the beauties leave it
and travel on through wastes of grief?
8.sharh: The beauties can strike camp and go. The lover is unsure his heart has the same freedom, especially since the country ahead of it is a wilderness of grief.

translation: They walk like gazelles, setting hearts swaying.
My gaze faltered. It could see and yet was blind.
9.sharh: Their movement seems to pass directly into the hearts of those who watch. The speaker’s eye can see the attraction perfectly well even as he loses all perspective on it.

translation: My heart flew to it. Reason warned my heart.
Grey hair rebuked me, “Give up this infatuation. Get up.”
10.sharh: Three voices now inhabit one man. The abrupt command to get up sounds like an attempt to wake him out of the love poem he has been telling.

translation: I spent the night listening to my heart whisper to me.
Reason liked my telling grey hair, “Go to sleep.”
11.sharh: The heart only has to whisper. Even reason, which issued the warning a moment ago, takes a liking to the convenient answer. “Sleep” neatly answers the earlier “Get up.”

translation: Like a wine drinker sipping in the name of God
to fend off drunkenness before the harm and regret.
12.sharh: The drinker says the devotional formula “in the name of God” while taking the very drink whose effects he hopes to escape. The lover recognises his own convenient piety in the gesture.

translation: No rite held off drunkenness after his impulse,
nor did wine and draughts of it slake his recklessness.
13.sharh: The pious gesture fails to undo the drink, and more wine fails to satisfy the impulse either. The last Arabic word means mouthfuls, making each return to the cup almost visible.

translation: I wish I knew whether his deed earns him a reward
or his ghouls have struck him deaf.
14.sharh: The thought of reward is ironic. The word for the ill effects of wine in verse 12 now finds an echo in the ghouls that have supposedly deafened the drinker to advice.

translation: The women’s promise is dust that rises and then subsides.
Once the cloud cleared, it disclosed an illusion.
15.sharh: A dust cloud at a distance might mean that someone is on the way. The lover has supplied the approaching figure himself, as he discovers when the dust settles.

translation: Do not be fooled. I have had experience of them.
Does a mirage ever meet the spot where your foot lands?
16.sharh: The test is as simple as putting a foot on the spot. What looked like water cannot be made to coincide with any piece of ground the traveller reaches.

translation: After grey hair appeared in me, blazing,
and its glow lit a heart that had strayed in darkness,
17.sharh: The blazing of grey hair recalls Zechariah’s prayer in Qur’an 19:4. This flame gives light to a wayward heart, and the unfinished question carries that hard-won clarity into the next verse.

translation: can desire still call you? Beware its changing colours,
a guileful chameleon blending grave wrong with small lapses.
18.sharh: The chameleon’s disguise is a change of moral scale. A serious wrong is easier to approach if it first takes on the colour of a passing lapse.

translation: Rein in desire, for your life is departing.
Youthful infatuation diminishes faith and character.
19.sharh: Grey hair has regained the authority that the lover tried to put to sleep. He now judges his infatuation by what it costs a person whose lifetime is already moving on.

translation: God bless grey hair. How much wisdom it holds
to clear our inward sight in bewilderment and darkness.
20.sharh: The older voice he once brushed aside has become a source of light. Inward sight answers the lover’s earlier confession that his perfectly good eyes had left him blind.

translation: Your world races past like a lone traveller on a horse,
swift as lightning, headstrong, with no check or bridle.
21.sharh: The horse has the speed of a lightning flash. The rider is on the horse, but has neither the means nor the strength to decide its pace.

translation: Be wary when the days make peace with you.
One day they praise you, then satirise you in the echo.
22.sharh: The days can flatter like a praise poet and wound like a satirist. The reversal is so swift the original praise still seems to be echoing.

translation: If youth makes you proud in its spring pastures,
the millstone of days drives you out through age.
23.sharh: Youth offers green places to settle in. The turning millstone brings another motion into that peaceful scene and grinds away the young person’s tenure.

translation: Do not lean on time when it draws near.
Beware. Its reversals honour no pledges.
24.sharh: Fortune acts like someone offering friendship. Its favour can draw a person close, yet the changing days recognise no obligation to keep a promise.

translation: One night it gives you sweet honey to drink. Tomorrow
you lie dust-covered among worms and crumbling bones.
25.sharh: “Tomorrow” arrives before the break between the halves. The shift from honey in the mouth to earth over the body is given no time to soften.

translation: The armour you laid up will never shield you
when the daughters of time wound you with their blows.
26.sharh: The “daughters of time” are its calamities. Even a store of armour, the most tangible protection he can imagine, cannot secure him against everything the future brings.

translation: All events, every one of them, have been written
with the Pen on the Tablet before the Almighty, exalted is He.
27.sharh: The Tablet and the Pen belong to the Islamic account of divine decree. The brief “exalted is He” interrupts the sentence to honour the One before whom the writing stands.

translation: What reaches you is a judgement none can undo.
What passes you by counts for you as though it never was.
28.sharh: The speaker draws attention away from the imagined life that might have been. What actually reaches a person is the portion with which that person can live and act.

translation: Only prayer wards off a judgement fixed or a fate decreed.
Seek refuge with God from afflictions.
29.sharh: The line echoes a prophetic report about supplication and decree. In this devotional understanding prayer is itself among the means God provides against affliction.

translation: No provision, no gift has brought you such happiness
as contentment, which enriches everyone who receives a share.
30.sharh: The gift that enriches every recipient is an attitude to the other gifts. A share can remain small and still cease to feel like a deprivation.

translation: A man spoiled by wealth dies in sandals of gold.
A servant in a rag digs the niche in his grave.
31.sharh: Gold sandals mark the distance between master and servant in life. At burial their positions change, and the man in rags makes the niche in which the rich man will lie.

translation: A rag has never made a repentant, devout man wretched,
nor has pride profited the peoples who have perished.
32.sharh: The verse refuses to read a person’s standing from his clothes. The scale widens from one poor servant to whole peoples whose pride bought them no lasting advantage.

translation: Be at ease in contentment’s palaces and live there a king.
Be content, give freely and hold fast to God’s rope.
33.sharh: Contentment changes who can be called a king. The final image of holding fast to God’s rope recalls Qur’an 3:103 and gives the heart, captive at the outset, something it can freely choose to hold.

1.1.4.head: رَدِيَ
1.1.4.meaning: To perish or come close to perishing.

1.2.2.head: خامَرَ
1.2.2.meaning: To mingle with something, to enter into it.

1.2.4.head: غَيداء
1.2.4.meaning: A graceful woman whose movements have a supple softness.

2.2.6.head: حِمَم
2.2.6.meaning: Pieces of charcoal or live embers.

3.1.3.head: مُعَنّى
3.1.3.meaning: Troubled or worn down by suffering.

4.2.4.head: شَذو
4.2.4.meaning: The diffusion of a sweet fragrance.

5.1.4.head: فَتَّ
5.1.4.meaning: To crumble or wear down, here an inward gnawing pain.

6.1.4.head: لَمياء
6.1.4.meaning: A woman with the dark tint inside the lips admired in classical Arabic descriptions.

6.2.5.head: عُروَة
6.2.5.meaning: A loop, tie or handhold by which something is held fast.

7.1.3.head: سامَرَ
7.1.3.meaning: To keep someone company in conversation by night.

7.1.5.head: نادَمَ
7.1.5.meaning: To share a drink as companions.

9.1.2.head: ريم
9.1.2.meaning: A pale gazelle admired for its graceful movement.

9.1.4.head: مادَ
9.1.4.meaning: To sway or rock from side to side.

10.2.4.head: صَبا
10.2.4.meaning: To give way to youthful desire or frivolity.

12.1.4.head: بَسمَلَة
12.1.4.meaning: Basmala is saying “In the name of God”.

12.2.4.head: غَول
12.2.4.meaning: The injurious effect of wine on the body or mind.

13.1.4.head: نُسك
13.1.4.meaning: A religious observance or act of devotion.

13.2.5.head: نُغمَة
13.2.5.meaning: A mouthful of drink. The studio gloss distinguishes nugham, “draughts”, from nagham, “melody”.

14.1.1-2.head: لَيتَ شِعري
14.1.1-2.meaning: “Would that I knew.” An established way of introducing a question.

14.2.3.head: غول
14.2.3.meaning: A ghoul, a creature of folklore said to lead people astray.

15.1.2.head: غانِيَة
15.1.2.meaning: A woman whose beauty is said to need no adornment.

15.1.3.head: نَقع
15.1.3.meaning: A cloud of dust raised into the air.

16.2.4.head: مَوطِئ
16.2.4.meaning: The spot where a foot comes down.

19.2.5.head: شيمَة
19.2.5.meaning: A trait of character or settled disposition.

20.1.1-2.head: لِلَّهِ دَرُّهُ
20.1.1-2.meaning: An Arabic expression of praise and admiration.

21.1.3.head: مُنبَتّ
21.1.3.meaning: A traveller cut off on the journey, traditionally one who has overdriven his mount.

21.2.6.head: لِجام
21.2.6.meaning: A bridle, the means by which a rider checks or steers a horse.

22.1.3.head: مُوادَعَة
22.1.3.meaning: A truce or agreement to leave one another in peace.

25.2.6.head: رِمَّة
25.2.6.meaning: A decayed bone, hence mortal remains.

26.2.3-4.head: بَنات الدَّهر
26.2.3-4.meaning: “The daughters of time” are the calamities it brings.

27.2.5.head: اللَّوح
27.2.5.meaning: Al-Lawh is the Preserved Tablet on which, in Islamic belief, God’s decrees are written.

28.2.2.head: عَدا
28.2.2.meaning: To pass someone by or miss them.

31.2.1.head: لَحَدَ
31.2.1.meaning: To dig the burial niche in the side of a grave.

33.2.3-4.head: حَبل اللَّه
33.2.3-4.meaning: “God’s rope” is the bond to which believers hold fast in Qur’an 3:103.
